lessons.title: Build a main sentence
lessons.rule: In a statement, the conjugated verb takes position two. Position means the second sentence element, which can be more than one word.
lessons.pattern: First element + conjugated verb + subject (if needed) + rest

example.german: Heute lerne ich zu Hause Deutsch.
example.english: Today I am learning German at home.

lessons.memory: Move a time phrase to the front; the verb stays second, so the subject moves after it.

check.prompt: Put these parts in order: morgen / wir / fahren / nach Berlin.
check.why: Morgen is the first element, fahren is second, and wir follows the verb.

lessons.title: Ask a clear question
lessons.rule: A yes/no question starts with the conjugated verb. A W-question starts with its question word, followed by the verb.

example.german: Kommst du heute? Wo wohnst du?
example.english: Are you coming today? Where do you live?

lessons.memory: Yes/no: verb first. W-question: question word first, verb second.

check.why: A yes/no question begins with the conjugated verb arbeitest.

lessons.title: Choose the right case
lessons.rule: A noun’s role helps determine its case. The verb or preposition can also govern the case, so ask what the phrase is doing in this sentence.
lessons.pattern: Der Mann (who?) + gibt + dem Kind (to whom?) + den Ball (what?)

example.german: Der Mann gibt dem Kind den Ball.
example.english: The man gives the child the ball.

lessons.memory: Wer/was? Nominativ · wem? Dativ · wen/was? Akkusativ · wessen? Genitiv.

check.prompt: In the example, who receives the ball, and what is being given?
check.answer: Dem Kind receives it (Dativ); den Ball is what is given (Akkusativ).
check.why: Geben commonly uses the pattern jemand gibt jemandem etwas. The full case tables and practice are in Cases Master.

lessons.title: Learn nouns with their article
lessons.rule: Store each noun with its grammatical gender and plural form. German noun gender is not always predictable from meaning.
lessons.pattern: das Buch → die Bücher  ·  der Tisch → die Tische  ·  die Lampe → die Lampen

example.german: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
example.english: The book is on the table.

lessons.memory: Learn the whole set: article + noun + plural. Say it aloud as one unit.

check.prompt: Recall the article and plural: Buch.
check.why: The article and plural are part of the word you are learning, not optional extras.

lessons.title: Talk about the past
lessons.rule: In everyday conversation, finished events often use Perfekt: a present-tense auxiliary plus a past participle at the end. Many verbs use haben; many intransitive verbs of movement or change use sein.

example.german: Gestern bin ich nach Berlin gefahren.

lessons.memory: The helper carries the tense; the participle closes the clause. Check the verb to choose haben or sein.

check.why: Ankommen describes arrival, a change of location, and uses sein here.

lessons.title: Say what is not true
lessons.rule: Use kein to negate an indefinite or unmarked noun. Use nicht to negate a verb, adjective, or specific phrase; its position depends on what you are negating.
lessons.pattern: Ich habe kein Auto.  ·  Ich kaufe das Auto nicht.

example.german: Ich habe heute keine Zeit, aber ich komme morgen.
example.english: I don’t have time today, but I’m coming tomorrow.

lessons.memory: kein goes with a noun; nicht negates the action or another specific part.

check.why: The sentence negates the action of coming, so it uses nicht.

lessons.title: Connect two ideas
lessons.rule: After subordinating words such as weil, dass, and wenn, the conjugated verb goes to the end of that clause. Put a comma between the clauses.

example.german: Weil es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.
example.english: Because it is raining, I am staying at home.

lessons.memory: The connector sends its clause’s verb to the end. After that clause, the main verb returns to position two.

check.prompt: Complete: Ich gehe früh ins Bett, weil ich müde ___.
check.answer: Ich gehe früh ins Bett, weil ich müde bin.
check.why: Weil introduces the subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb bin goes at the end.

lessons.title: Use modal verbs
lessons.rule: Conjugate the modal verb in position two and put the main verb in the infinitive at the end.

example.english: I have to work longer today.

lessons.memory: One verb is conjugated in the middle; the other waits at the end.

check.why: Kann is the conjugated modal; sprechen stays infinitive at the end.
